newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel says Arafat still not fighting "terrorists".
newsitem.headline: Israel says Arafat still not fighting "terrorists".

text.p: Israel said on Tuesday that Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat had yet to act against anti-Israeli militants six days after suicide bombers blew up a Jewish market in Jerusalem.
"Without these demands being met, the peace process between them and us is in danger," Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told reporters at an army induction base in Tel Aviv.

Egypt and Jordan -- Arab states at peace with Israel -- led a diplomatic drive to save Israeli-PLO peacemaking from a crisis which deepened with the blasts last Wednesday that killed 15 people, including the two bombers, and wounded 170.
"The truth is there is no action by the (Palestinian) Authority against the infrastructure of the terrorist groups," Netanyahu said. "To my regret, it's also true at this moment."

Israeli spokesman David Bar-Illan said Palestinian President Yasser Arafat had yet to arrest leaders of "terrorist" military wings or to try to disarm them or to extradite 31 Palestinians to Israel wanted for killing Israelis.

Since the attack, Israel has imposed a closure on the West Bank and Gaza Strip, arrested 156 militants in areas under its control and threatened to enter Palestinian self-rule areas to fight militants if Arafat did not do the job.
Palestinians have said the Israeli measures are collective punishments that weaken Arafat and strengthen extremist forces.

The bombers in the latest attack have yet to be identified. A leaflet issued in the name of the Islamist Hamas group claimed responsibility but Israeli and PLO officials have questioned its authenticity.
Middle Eastern leaders crisscrossed the region in search of a way out of the crisis. In Amman late on Monday, Arafat met Jordan's King Hussein, who was due to meet Netanyahu in Israel on Wednesday.
Arafat and Netanyahu haven't met each other for months.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy met Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak in Cairo, and U.S. President Bill Clinton's Middle East envoy Dennis Ross was due in the region at the weekend.

Ross had planned a Middle East mission last week but delayed the visit for a period of Israeli mourning following the attack. Israeli-PLO talks already were stuck over Netanyahu's expansion of Jewish settlements and a surge of violence.
In Amman, Arafat accused Netanyahu of wrecking the peace process and humiliating the Palestinians in the wake of last week's suicide bombings.

He told reporters after talks with Prime Minister Abdul Salam al-Majali that his security bosses had told him that even Israeli intelligence pointed to the suicide bombers coming from outside Palestinian self-rule areas.
"So clearly the objective and aim is to wreck the peace process and the objective and aim is to humilitiate the Palestinian people," Arafat said angrily.
Arafat also attacked Netanyahu personally, saying the Israeli leader was still a political novice who had still to learn much about dealing with the Palestinians.
Palestinians suspended security cooperation with Israel after Netanyahu broke ground on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem in March.

A senior Israeli official, briefing reporters on security since the bombing, said the Palestinian Authority so far had limited its cooperation to the investigation of the attack. Palestinian police had made some arrests also.

"They are coordinating and exercising cooperation in the investigation about the last bombing," the official said. "They are not doing their best in actions against the infrastructure of the whole terror organisation, especially Hamas, the (Islamic) Jihad (group) and the Popular Front."

The official, familiar with details of the investigation into Wednesday's attack, said it was still not clear who the suicide bombers were, what type of explosives had been used or whether they had come from abroad.
"Their clothes had no labels in them. They took them off," the official said. "I think it was well-prepared (and) for a long time. They paid attention to all the small details," the official said.
